title: I Believe in Bigfoot and Other Travel Qualifications
excerpt: A summer of bad directions, good omens, and places worth pulling over for.
content:
Let’s get this out of the way: I believe in Bigfoot.

You may do with that what you want.

I believe in Bigfoot with the seriousness of someone who recently purchased the Bigfoot Magazine Newsweek special edition on eBay and felt, if anything, undercharged. This is the hill I will die on. Preferably near a tree line, with questionable footprints nearby.

I also think cemeteries are excellent lunch spots. Calm. Quiet. Usually scenic. Very few people asking you to move.

I have never seen a ghost, which frankly feels rude given the amount of emotional availability I have brought to the situation. I believe déjà vu is what happens when another dimension brushes against ours and pretends it didn’t. I trust old signs. I respect a roadside attraction. I think abandoned objects are usually trying to tell us something.

So no, I am probably not the person you send to write a normal travel diary.

Which is useful, because this summer I’ve been dared to investigate my own backyard with Atlas Obscura.

I was born and raised in California, which means I have spent most of my life thinking I know this place, only to be corrected by it constantly. California is a fever dream with parking, except in Los Angeles, where the parking is also part of the fever dream. Desert. Ocean. Forest. Freeway. Strip mall. Neon. Dust. Glamour. Ruin. Reinvention. Repeat.

It is a state where the strange does not always announce itself. Sometimes it is huge and roaring on the side of the highway. Sometimes it is quiet, broken-looking, and still waiting for someone to pick up the receiver.

Like a payphone.

My own project, The Goodbye Line, began with a search for the last working payphones we could find across Los Angeles. What I learned is that once you start looking for overlooked things, the map changes. Corners become clues. Gas stations become archives. Old objects become invitations. You realize that America is full of things that are not exactly gone, just waiting for someone to notice they are still working.

That is the spirit I’m bringing into this summer with Atlas Obscura.

I’m following the places in California that ask for a second look: the half-lit sign, the last working machine, the roadside object with a backstory, the room someone has been unlocking for decades.

And more than the places, I’m looking for the people attached to them.

The caretakers. The collectors. The unofficial historians. The person with the key. The person who knows what everyone gets wrong. The person who keeps showing up after the novelty wears off, to sweep the floor, answer the phone, repaint the sign, tell the story one more time.

Follow along. I can’t promise this will be educational in the typical sense, but I can promise it will be interesting. Roadside giants may appear. Cemetery lunches are likely. Questionable signage feels inevitable. At least one thing will probably be treated as a portal.

Maybe that is my real map of California this summer: not highways or county lines, but a trail of people caring for things the rest of us almost forgot to see.
